_comment: Slavic genii, fate-spirits, water/forest beings and festival rites cut from Machal, Slavic Mythology (Mythology of All Races III, 1918), Parts I and IV. All passages paraphrase.

title.en: The Zduhacz: Sleep-Souls Battling on the Mountain
title.zh: 茲杜哈茨：山頂之魂的征戰

region.zh: 蒙特內哥羅（象徵性定位於洛夫琴山）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1

summary.en: In Serbian and Montenegrin belief the soul leaves a sleeper's body as a Zduhacz, a winged guardian-genius; all the Zduhaczs of a region must fight on a mountain-top each spring, and whichever side wins brings its homeland rain, rich harvest, and healthy herds.
summary.zh: 塞爾維亞與蒙特內哥羅信仰中，靈魂於睡眠時化身茲杜哈茨守護精靈；各族之魂靈於山頂交戰，勝者一方賜其鄉土雨水、豐收與牛羊興旺。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief recorded by ethnographers; no living-community restrictions.

passages.text: In Serbian and Montenegrin belief a person's soul can leave the sleeping body and fly abroad as a Zduhacz, a guardian-genius; even the souls of cats, dogs, and oxen may become Zduhaczs. On mountain-tops the genii of every land assemble and battle with one another, man against man and troop against troop. The victors bring their countrymen rich harvest and success in breeding cattle; if a man's soul is slain in the fight, he never wakes again.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: In Montenegro the Zduhaczs of land and sea are distinguished: those of land cause drought, those of sea bring rain, and the weather of the year depends on which of the two prevails. A sudden storm betrays a battle among them. A man with such a soul is said to know all that passes at a distance, for he has seen it while flying abroad in sleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mora: Night-Demon of the Slavic Household
title.zh: 摩拉：斯拉夫家宅的夜魔

region.zh: 斯拉夫諸地（象徵性定位於基輔）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1

summary.en: A Mora is a living person whose soul leaves the body at night to torment sleepers: sent as straw, shadow, cat, mouse, or snake, she first lulls her victims with sweet slumber, then chokes them in terrible dreams and drinks their blood.
summary.zh: 摩拉乃活人之靈夜間出竅作祟：化為稻草、陰影、貓鼠或蛇，先使人酣眠，繼而噩夢窒息、吮其血。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; the Mora figure survives in modern Slavic fairy tales without community restrictions.

passages.text: The Slavs widely believe that certain living persons, man or woman, may be a Mora: the soul leaves the sleeping body at night and returns at dawn. Such a person may be known from birth by bushy black eyebrows that meet above the nose. The Mora takes many shapes — a piece of straw, a white shadow, a leather bag, a white mouse, a cat, a snake, or a white horse — and comes by night to the dwellings of men.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: She first sends refreshing slumber to those within, and then, when they sleep, torments them with terrible dreams, chokes them, and sucks their blood. Children are her chief victims, but she attacks horses and cattle too, and withers trees. In Russia the Mora becomes the Kikimora, a tiny household demon that lives behind the oven: at night it whines and whistles, spins endlessly, and tangles the tow of any spinner who fails to make the sign of the cross.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The Vlkodlak: Werewolf and Eater of the Sun
title.zh: 維爾科拉克：狼人與吞日者

region.en: Southern Slavic lands (symbolic pin at Sarajevo)
region.zh: 南斯拉夫諸地（象徵性定位於薩拉熱窩）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1

summary.en: The Vlkodlak is a man transformed into a wolf by magic, often a bride or bridegroom enchanted on the wedding road; a dark Southern-Slav tradition makes the werewolf chase the clouds and devour the sun or moon, so that drums, bells, and gunfire are raised to drive him from the light.
summary.zh: 維爾科拉克乃受魔術化狼之人，多為婚途上新娘新郎；南斯拉夫古傳其追雲吞日食月致蝕，故鳴鼓敲鐘放炮以驅之。

sensitivity.note: The eclipse-demon parallels the wolf that devours sun or moon in Norse, Chinese, and other traditions; tagging is interpretive.

passages.text: A child born feet first, or born with teeth, may become a Vlkodlak — a werewolf; more often a man is turned into one by the magic of another, and this happens most frequently to the bride and bridegroom as they go to the church to be married. The enchanted one runs about the village as a wolf, gazing plaintively at the people he once knew but harming no one, until the same enchanter destroys the charm.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Among the Southern Slavs a tradition dating from the thirteenth century tells of a Vukodlak who followed the clouds and devoured the sun or the moon, causing an eclipse. On such an occasion the people beat drums, ring bells, and fire guns to drive the demon from the light. By night the Vlkodlak also attacks cattle, sucks the milk of cows and mares, and strangles horses.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The Vampire: Unquiet Dead of the Slavs
title.zh: 吸血鬼：斯拉夫之不寧亡者

region.zh: 巴爾幹（象徵性定位於貝爾格勒）

texts.period: Belief attested from 11th c.; recorded 19th c. (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1

summary.en: Sorcerers, suicides, and the violently dead cannot rest: their bodies are occupied by an unclean spirit, do not decay, and rise at night to wail on wayside crosses and drain the blood of the living until cock-crow; villages end the plague by digging up the corpse and staking and burning it.
summary.zh: 巫者、自盡者與橫死之人不得安息：屍身被穢靈所據，不腐不敗，夜起於十字架上哀哭、吸吮生人之血，雞鳴乃止；村人掘屍穿椿焚之，以絕其害。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; keep in myth category (legendary) rather than folklore-verbatim testimony of real events.

passages.text: Among the Slavs the souls of sorcerers, great sinners, suicides, and the violently dead are loath to part with their bodies and return to trouble the living; such corpses were long denied churchyard burial and thrown into pits or swamps. From such graves rise the Vampires — the dead occupied by an unclean spirit, a belief traceable as far back as the eleventh century.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.

passages.text: Any person over whom a dog or cat jumps, or upon whom an unclean shadow falls, may become a vampire after death; the corpse does not decay but keeps the colour of life. At night the vampire leaves the grave, rocks and wails upon wayside crosses, and sucks the blood of people and cattle until cock-crow ends his power. Villages defend themselves by exhuming the body, driving an ashen or hawthorn stake through its heart, and burning it.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 1; not verbatim.

title.en: The Ship-Pyre of a Rus Chieftain: Ibn Fadlan's Account
title.zh: 羅斯酋長的船葬火焚：伊本·法德蘭所記

region.en: Volga river, lands of the Volga Rus (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 伏爾加河羅斯人之地（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Eyewitness account of 922 (Ibn Fadlan); retold by Machal 1918

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2, retelling Ahmad ibn Fadlan's risala of 922

summary.en: The Arab envoy Ibn Fadlan watched the funeral of a Rus chieftain on the Volga: the dead man's ship was hauled ashore, an old woman called the Angel of Death stabbed a slave girl who had volunteered to follow her lord, and all was burned in a ship-pyre crowned with days of feasting.
summary.zh: 阿拔斯使節伊本·法德蘭親見伏爾加河畔羅斯酋長葬禮：船屍上岸，老嫗名『死神天使』者刺殺自願殉葬之婢，船焚火起，宴飲連日。

sensitivity.note: Historical eyewitness account including ritual killing; treated soberly at ethnographic level as funerary religion, without graphic detail.

passages.text: When a nobleman of the Rus on the Volga died, his body lay in a provisional grave for ten days while a shroud was prepared. His property was divided three ways: a third to the family, a third for the funeral, and a third spent on the strong drink of the funeral banquet. On the appointed day a boat was drawn from the water, and the corpse, clad in costly garments, was seated in it upon a richly ornamented armchair, surrounded by his weapons, bread, fruit, and the flesh of sacrificed dogs, horses, cows, and fowls.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2, from Ibn Fadlan (922); not verbatim.

passages.text: One of the dead man's wives had consented to die with him; an old woman called the Angel of Death conducted the rite at the boat's side, and after the sacrifice the wood piled beneath was fired. When ship, bodies, and offerings were consumed, the ashes were gathered and strewn over a cairn, and the ceremony closed with banqueting day and night without interruption.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.

title.en: The Dziady: Feeding the Ancestors of White Russia
title.zh: 吉亞迪：白俄羅斯的祭祖宴

region.en: White Russia / Belarus (symbolic pin at Minsk)
region.zh: 白俄羅斯（象徵性定位於明斯克）

texts.period: Rite recorded 19th c.; pre-Christian in origin (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2

summary.en: Four times a year the Belarusian Dziady bring the forefathers home: the house is scrubbed, a pail of water and a wisp of straw are set out for the dead to wash, the housefather invites the 'holy Dziadys' to the meal, and any rustle of leaves or drifting moth is greeted as their coming.
summary.zh: 白俄羅斯人一年四度行吉亞迪祭：灑掃家宅，置水與草束供亡魂盥洗，家主恭請『神聖祖靈』赴宴；風動葉響、蛾影飄至，皆視為先人臨門。

sensitivity.note: Living rite descended from ancestor cult; described at ethnographic level only.

passages.text: The autumnal Dziady fall on the eve of St. Demetrius, when the harvest is in. The courtyard is swept, tools stowed, and a beast set aside since spring is killed; the women cook from nine to fifteen dishes and scrub the room, giving special care to the corner behind the oven, the most important place in the house. A plentiful board and a clean house are thought to please the souls of the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: In the evening the family bathes, sets out a pail of fresh water with a wisp of straw for the Dziadys to wash in, and assembles in Sunday best. The housefather lights a candle in a corner, prays, and solemnly invites the holy Dziadys to the meal. Before eating he sets a portion of every dish on a plate in the window; spoons are laid on the table for the ancestors to help themselves. A rustle of dry leaves, a stirring of air, even the appearance of an emperor-moth is taken for the coming of the forefathers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: At the spring Dziady, called radunica, the family carries food to the churchyard on the Tuesday of Easter week: the women chant dirges, the men roll priest-blessed eggs, a cloth is spread on the grave, and the circle sits about it eating and talking of the dead, leaving the remains to beggars or the grave itself. The summer Dziady, on the Saturday before Whitsunday, sweep the graves with birch twigs — 'giving the Dziadys a steam-bath'.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.

title.en: The Stopan's Feast: A Bulgarian Ancestor Guards the House
title.zh: 斯托潘之宴：保加利亞家宅祖靈

region.zh: 保加利亞（象徵性定位於索菲亞）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2

summary.en: In Bulgarian belief a Stopan — a valiant dead ancestor — guards the family home; at his yearly feast a black hen's blood is poured into the hearth hollow, cakes are cut and set in three corners of the loft with wine, and the family prays the Stopan for flocks, meadows, and vineyards.
summary.zh: 保加利亞人信家中斯托潘乃勇武先祖之靈；歲宴宰黑雞、血灑爐膛，切餅置酒於閣樓三角，闔家祈其佑羊群、草場與葡萄園。

sensitivity.note: Living ancestral rite described at ethnographic level.

passages.text: The Bulgarian Stopan is a deceased ancestor, distinguished for valour in his lifetime, who guards the house of the family: he secures health and long life, makes the sheep multiply, promotes harvests, and fills vineyards and orchards. His only price is honour and sufficient food; if the family neglects him, hail may ruin the fields and whole households come to ruin.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: At his feast the house is scrubbed, candles are lit by the hearth and door, and the oldest woman kills a black hen so that the blood flows into the hollow of the hearth, which is then smeared with clay. The head of the family pours half a cup of wine into the fire, cuts a cake into four parts while leaping about the room, and sets the gifts — buttered cake, the hen's left leg, three cups of wine — in three corners of the loft, praying the Stopan to guard the flocks, the meadows, and the vineyards.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 2; not verbatim.

title.en: Dedushka Domovoy: The House-Lord Behind the Oven
title.zh: 多莫沃伊祖父：爐後家主

region.en: Russia (symbolic pin at a northern village)
region.zh: 俄羅斯（象徵性定位於北方村落）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3

summary.en: Every Russian house has its Domovoy, a grizzled ancestral 'Grandfather' hairy as a beast, who lives behind the oven, tends the herds, weeps at night when death or calamity is coming — and must be carried to a new home in a pan of hot cinders when the family moves.
summary.zh: 俄家宅皆有其多莫沃伊：毛髮灰白之『祖父』居於爐後，照看牛馬；家有大故，夜半嗚咽預警；遷居時以炭火之盤恭迎其隨行。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; the Domovoy is a beloved figure of Russian tales without restriction.

passages.text: Dedushka Domovoy, the House-Lord, is an old man with a grizzled bushy head, flashing eyes, and a body covered in thick soft hair, wearing a long cloak with a light red belt. He takes the shape of the master of the house, living or dead — or of a cat, dog, or bear whose coat matches the master's hair — and lives behind the oven, under the threshold, or in the stable, doing the master's work at night and guarding the herds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Domovoy shares the joy and sorrow of his home: if an inmate dies he howls at night, and bitter sobbing foretells the master's own death or a coming fire or plague. Angered by cursing or neglect, he may quit the house and let the cattle sicken and the family die. His favour is courted with the leftovers of supper, and an angry Domovoy is reconciled with the blood of a cock killed at midnight, or with bread and salt wrapped in white cloth while the household bows to the four quarters.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: When a family moves to a new house they never forget to take the Domovoy with them. An old woman heats the stove in the old house, puts the cinders in a clean pan covered with a napkin, and at the open window invites the spirit to come; at the gate of the new home the master and mistress wait with bread and salt, bowing low and asking him to enter. The coals are emptied into the new oven and the pan buried beneath the front corner of the room.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.

title.en: The Skritek: Hatching the Household Goblin
title.zh: 斯克里特克：孵出的小妖

region.zh: 波希米亞（象徵性定位於布拉格）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3

summary.en: The Czech Skritek — a crowned wooden figure kept on the chiffonier — guards the house and brings grain and riches, but can also be hatched from an odd egg carried under the arm, and can be hired for a terrible price: one's own self, wife, and children, pledged in one's own blood.
summary.zh: 捷克斯克里特克——冠冕木像置於櫃上——守家賜穀致富；亦可由腋下孵化怪蛋而生；若欲其效力，須以己血簽契，獻上己身、妻、子。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: The Czech Skritek, a hobgoblin like a small boy, lives behind the oven or in the stable, favours the household, weaves on the loom, sweeps the floor, and tends the flocks. He is represented by a wooden statue with crossed arms and a crown, set in the corner behind the table to guard the house in the family's absence. He may be bred from an egg of peculiar shape carried for a time beneath the armpit; in Poland his bird-form, a drenched chicken trailing wings and tail, flies by night scattering sparks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: He brings the householder grain and riches — when he carries money he flies down the chimney like a fiery broom — but his help has a price: one must promise him one's own self, wife, and children, signing the agreement in one's own blood. Millet gruel must always be left for him on the window-sill; three bits of every dish are his at the Christmas dinner, and if they are forgotten he storms and worries the household and wastes the flocks.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 3; not verbatim.

title.en: The Sudice: Three Destinies at the Cradle
title.zh: 蘇迪采：搖籃邊的三命運女神

region.en: Bohemia and South Slavic lands (symbolic pin at Prague)
region.zh: 波希米亞與南斯拉夫（象徵性定位於布拉格）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4

summary.en: On the night after a birth the Sudice come: white-robed, candle-bearing genii of fate who spin, measure, and cut the thread of the new-born's life; the last and oldest speaks decisively, and only gifts of bread, salt, and candles left on the table can soften the verdict.
summary.zh: 嬰兒誕生之夜，蘇迪采降臨：白衣持燭之命運精靈，紡線、量線、斷線以定一生；最末者最老，一言定讞；桌上麵包、鹽與燭乃軟化判語之禮。

sensitivity.note: Fate-spirits parallel the Greek Moirai and Norse Norns; interpretive tagging.

passages.text: The genii of fate — Sudice among the Czechs, Rodjenice among the Croats and Slovenes, Orisnici among the Bulgarians, Udelnicy in northern Russia — come to the bedside of a woman in childbed after casting her into deep sleep, set the new-born on the table, and decide its fate: how long it will live, whether it will be rich or poor, and what manner of death it will die. Usually they are three, the third and oldest the most powerful; what the last says is decisive and will be fulfilled.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4; not verbatim.

passages.text: They appear as beautiful lasses or kindly old women, white-robed, veiled, bearing burning candles. One spins, the second measures, and the third cuts off the thread whose length is the span of life. Their favour can be won: on the night after the birth the Slovenes and Croats set wax candles, wine, bread, and salt on the lying-in room's table; the Bulgarians prepare a supper for the Orisnici; in Bohemia a table was spread with white cloth, bread, salt, butter, cheese, and beer.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4; not verbatim.

title.en: Dolya and Nedolya: The Woman Who Is One's Fate
title.zh: 多利亞與內多利亞：化身命運的女子

region.zh: 俄羅斯（象徵性定位於諾夫哥羅德）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4

summary.en: Russian folk belief personifies each person's lot as Dolya, a poorly-dressed woman who lives behind the oven: a good Dolya labours invisibly for her man all his days, while an evil Nedolya sleeps, dresses, and laughs — and no horse can carry a man away from her.
summary.zh: 俄俗以『多利亞』喻人之一生命定：衣衫襤褸之婦居於爐後；善者日夜為其人勞作，惡者（內多利亞）唯睡、妝、嬉戲——諺云：駿馬亦載不走你的命。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: Russian tradition makes the fate given a man at his birth a supernatural woman, Dolya, poorly dressed and able to change her shape, living behind the oven. A good Dolya protects her favourite day and night from birth to death: she waters his fields with dew, drives fish into his nets and swarms of bees into his hives, guards his flocks against wild beasts, finds buyers for his goods, and picks the full ears from other men's sheaves for him. Without her help no one succeeds.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4; not verbatim.

passages.text: Woe to the man who draws an evil Dolya — Nedolya, or Licho. She does nothing but sleep, dress herself, and make merry, and all his labour is in vain; her power has no limits, and the proverb says 'not even your horse will get you away from your Dolya': selling her, losing her in the woods, drowning her in the sea — all fail. The Serbian counterpart, Sreca, is a beautiful girl spinning a golden thread for the man assigned to her; as Nesreca she is an old woman with bloodshot eyes, forever asleep.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 4; not verbatim.

title.en: The Mavky Cry: 'Mother Bore Me and Left Me Unbaptized'
title.zh: 瑪芙卡哭聲：『母生我而不洗禮』

region.zh: 烏克蘭（象徵性定位於基輔）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5

summary.en: Navky — souls of children unbaptized or drowned — rock on moonlit branches crying for baptism; whoever hears their wail and speaks the baptismal formula frees them, but after seven years unpitied they become dangerous water-nymphs.
summary.zh: 納芙基——未受洗或溺斃孩童之魂——月夜攀枝搖盪，哭求洗禮；聞其哀而誦洗禮經文者釋其靈；七年無人憐惜，遂化為索命水仙。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief entangling pagan water-spirits with Christian rite; tagged interpretively.

passages.text: The Little Russian Mavky is the soul of a child drowned by its mother or left unbaptized: a small baby, or a beautiful girl with curling hair, half-naked or in a white shirt. On moonlit nights she rocks on the branches of trees, imitating the crying of infants, laughing and clapping her hands to draw the young after her; whoever follows will be bewitched by her beauty, tickled to death, and drawn into deep water.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: In summer they swim in rivers beating the water merrily; in the fairy-week they run the fields and meadows wailing, 'Mother has borne me and left me unbaptized.' Whoever hears the cry and answers, 'I baptize thee in the name of God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit,' sets the soul free. But if for seven years no one pities them, they are turned into water-nymphs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5; not verbatim.

title.en: Rusalka Week: The Water-Nymphs Walk the Rye
title.zh: 羅薩爾卡週：水仙行於麥浪

region.en: Russia (symbolic pin on the Dnieper banks)
region.zh: 俄羅斯（象徵性定位於第聶伯河岸）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5

summary.en: Rusalky — drowned girls and unbaptized souls — rise at Whitsuntide to run the green corn, dance in moonlit fairy-rings, and tickle wanderers to death; for their week the villages bring no work into the fields and lay bread, cheese, and butter on the banks for them.
summary.zh: 羅薩爾卡——溺亡之女與未洗之魂——五旬節週起身，奔跑青麥、月下環舞、搔癢旅人致死；村人停田間之工，於河岸供麵包乳酪。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; Rusalka imagery is a classic of Slavic art and music.

passages.text: The Rusalky are girls who died unnaturally or unbaptized children, appearing as maidens seven years old or in the full bloom of youth, dressed in green leaves or in a white shirt without a belt. They live in woods, meadows, and waters; when the corn begins to ripen they hide in it ready to punish whoever plucks the ears wantonly, and at Whitsuntide they rock among the high-standing grain, making it wave.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5; not verbatim.

passages.text: On clear summer nights they rise from the streams to bathe and splash, sit on the mill-wheel crying 'Kuku', and dance on the banks, leaving fairy-rings of particularly deep green grass. They entangle fishermen's nets, break dikes to flood the fields, and lure wanderers to be tickled to death or drawn into the deep. During their week at Whitsuntide no one bathes, works the fields, or claps hands, and lads and lasses lay bread, cheese, and butter on the banks for them.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 5; not verbatim.

title.en: The Vily: Fairies Who Left When the Whips Were Cracked
title.zh: 維拉精靈：鞭聲響處，仙子離去

region.en: South Slavic mountains (symbolic pin in the Rhodopes)
region.zh: 南斯拉夫山地（象徵性定位於羅多彼山脈）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 6

summary.en: In the golden age the Vily helped mortals plough, sow, and bury their dead; when shepherds took to whips and cursing and the first guns were heard, the fairies left forever. Their life hangs in their golden hair — lose one hair and a Vila dies — and whoever steals her wings binds her to earth until she regains them.
summary.zh: 黃金時代維拉助人耕種葬亡；牧者一旦鞭撻咒詛、槍聲初響，仙子遂去不返。其命懸金髮——落一髮即亡；竊其羽者可繫之於世，羽還則逝。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; Vila lore is central to South Slavic epic.

passages.text: In the happy days when fields bore wheat without man's labour, the Vily helped mortals garner harvests, mow grass, feed cattle, and build houses; they taught men to plough, to sow, to drain meadows, even to bury the dead. But when men departed from their old virtues — when shepherds threw away flutes and songs, took up whips, and cursed; when the first guns were heard and nations made war — the Vily left the country for foreign lands. Now only a few ever see them dancing in the fields or sitting on a bare rock, weeping and singing melancholy songs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 6; not verbatim.

passages.text: The Vily are eternally young women, pale-cheeked, dressed in white, with long golden hair in which their life and strength reside: lose a single hair and she will die. Their eyes flash like lightning; their voices, once heard, are never forgotten. They ride horses and stags, live in clouds, on forest mountains, and in waters, and transform themselves into wolves, snakes, falcons, or swans. A man who robs a fairy of her pinions can bind her to himself; the moment she regains her wings she vanishes forever — though she still watches in secret over her children.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 6; not verbatim.

title.en: The Leshy: Lord of the Forest and His Echoes
title.zh: 雷希：林主與其回聲

region.zh: 俄羅斯森林帶（象徵性定位）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7

summary.en: The Leshy is an old man of the woods as tall as the trees he haunts, whose rustling walk and mocking echoes mislead travellers; his favourite is the bear, with whom he feasts, and he can be escaped only by putting the right shoe on the left foot and looking between one's legs.
summary.zh: 雷希乃林中老者，身高隨所棲之樹；行走時林木沙沙，慣以回聲戲弄迷途者；其寵為熊，與之宴樂；脫身之術乃右鞋穿左足、俯身跨腿回望。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: The Russian Leshy shows himself as an old man with long hair and beard, flashing green eyes, a body covered with hair, and the stature of the trees he inhabits — tree-high in the forest, grass-high in the field. He takes the shapes of bears, wolves, and hares, or appears to travellers as an ordinary person, even as their own friend. One Leshy rules each wood; a silvan czar is lord where several dwell.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.

passages.text: He guards the forest, forbidding whistling and shouting, frightening thieves with cries, and feasting with his favourite, the bear. When he walks, the trees rustle; he rocks on boughs, whistles, laughs, claps, cracks his whip, and neighs like a horse, lows like a cow, barks like a dog, mews like a cat — the echo is his work, and no man has ever found his footprints in sand or snow, for a strong wind always blows around him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.

passages.text: Of a mocking temper, he removes boundary-stones and signposts, takes the shape of a wanderer's friend to lure him into thickets and morasses, and substitutes his own ugly, voracious children for human infants. Salted bread wrapped in linen laid in the woods is his due offering; huntsmen leave him the first game. To escape his bewitchment one turns one's garments inside out, puts the right shoe on the left foot, or bends down to look between one's own legs.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.

title.en: The Wild Women of the Bohemian Woods
title.zh: 波希米亞林中的野婦

region.zh: 波希米亞／勞西茨（象徵性定位於布拉格）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7

summary.en: The Divozenky — large-headed, long-haired Wild Women — lived in burrows under the Bohemian woods, baking bread from gleaned ears and weaving hemp; they kept the houses of those who left them food, raised never-failing crops, and vanished if anyone called them 'Wild Women'.
summary.zh: 迪沃真卡——方顱長髮之野婦——穴居波希米亞林下，拾穗磨石、烘麵織麻；凡供食者彼為之灑掃理家，賜永不枯竭之收成；一經喚作『野婦』，即刻消失。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: In Bohemian and Lusatian belief the Wild Women (Divozenky, Dziwje Zony) were good-looking beings with large square heads, long ruddy or black hair, hairy bodies, and long fingers, living in underground burrows furnished like houses. They gleaned ears in the fields, ground grain between stones, and baked bread whose smell filled the whole wood; they combed and wove hemp into frocks and shirts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.

passages.text: They knew the secret forces of nature and anointed themselves with unguents to become light and invisible; their wild frolicking was blamed for storms. They entered villages to borrow kneading-troughs, and repaid kindness richly: they kept houses in order, swept rooms and courtyards, cared for children, reaped corn, and gave the women crops that never diminished. But they vanished at once if anyone called them 'Wild Women', or left a fireside uncleared.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 7; not verbatim.

title.en: Polednica: The Midday Spirit with the Sickle
title.zh: 波萊德尼察：持鐮的正午精靈

region.zh: 波希米亞／波蘭（象徵性定位於弗羅茨瓦夫）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 8

summary.en: At the burning noon of harvest a tall white-robed woman with a sickle walks the fields: Polednica sets riddles to the reapers, twists the necks of those found working at midday, and carries off children left alone in the standing corn.
summary.zh: 收割烈日當空，白衣高挑持鐮之婦行於田間：波萊德尼察向割麥人出謎，扭折正午勞作者之頸，奪走獨留麥浪之孩童。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; parallels the noon-demon of many traditions.

passages.text: In Bohemian belief the Poludnica is an airy white lady or an old woman who wanders the fields at noon, floating on violent gusts; whomsoever she touches will die a sudden death. Sometimes she is slight as a girl of twelve, whip in hand, striking anyone who crosses her path. She ambushes women lately become mothers who go out at midday, and carries off children left alone in the fields at harvest-time — hence mothers hush crying children with the threat that she is coming.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 8; not verbatim.

passages.text: In Polish belief she is a tall woman in a white robe to her feet, carrying a sharp sickle; she chases the workers of the fields and woods through summer, propounding hard questions to them and sending grievous maladies on those who cannot answer. Among the Lusatian Serbs whoever meets her in the fields at noon must talk with her for a full hour on a single subject; those who fail forfeit their heads. She guards the corn from thieves and punishes children who tread upon the ears.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 8; not verbatim.

title.en: Vodyanoy: The Water-Grandfather and His Hundred Daughters
title.zh: 沃吉亞諾伊：水祖父與百女

region.en: Russian rivers (symbolic pin on the Volga)
region.zh: 俄羅斯河川（象徵性定位於伏爾加河）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 9

summary.en: Vodyanoy, the bald water-grandfather with a reed crown and a coat that drips from the left side, keeps herds of horses and cattle in his underwater courtyards; when a river overflows its banks he is celebrating his wedding — drunk, and tearing down dikes and mills.
summary.zh: 沃吉亞諾伊——禿頂、戴蘆葦冠、左襟滴水之水祖父——於水底石院牧養馬牛豬群；江河氾濫之時，正是其婚宴酩酊、毀堤拆磨之日。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief; includes traditional foundation sacrifice motif described ethnographically.

passages.text: The Vodyanik, or Grandfather Vodyanoy, is a bald old man with fat belly, puffy cheeks, a high cap of reeds, and a belt of rushes; in the village he passes as a man, betrayed only by water oozing from the left side of his coat. He lives in the deep water near mills, where he keeps stone courtyards and herds of horses, cattle, sheep, and pigs driven out to graze at night.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 9; not verbatim.

passages.text: Master of the waters, terrible in his element and weak ashore, he drives fish into the nets of those he favours and wrecks the boats of those he does not; he tears spikes from mill-wheels and floods the mill, which is why a miller must bury a living being in the mill's foundations to make his dam endure. He has one hundred and eleven beautiful daughters who torment the drowned; when the waters rise over their banks he is celebrating his wedding, drunk, tearing down dikes and bridges.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 9; not verbatim.

passages.text: In spring he wakes hungry and troublesome, breaking the ice and howling; a horse smeared with honey is sacrificed to him, and for three days he awaits the gift, betraying his greed by heaving waters and dismal howls. Fishermen pour butter into the water; millers kill a black, well-fed sow in his honour.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 9; not verbatim.

title.en: Every Man a Star: The Falling Light of Death
title.zh: 人各有星：隕落之光即是死

region.zh: 斯拉夫諸地（象徵性定位於基輔）

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 10

summary.en: Slavic folk astronomy binds every human life to a star: there are as many stars as men, each person receives one at birth, and when the star falls the man dies and his soul floats up among the clouds.
summary.zh: 斯拉夫星象俗信：天上有幾星，人間有幾人；人誕生則得一星，星落則人亡，魂魄化光升於雲間。

sensitivity.note: Folk belief.

passages.text: Arabian travellers report that the pagan Slavs adored the sun, and an old Bohemian homilist records that they worshipped not only sun, moon, and stars, but water, fire, mountains, and trees. The moon was held to be the abode of the souls of the departed, later of sinful souls transported there by way of punishment, and popular belief gave her power over the growth of plants and beasts.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 10; not verbatim.

passages.text: All Slavs maintain a close relationship between stars and men: there are as many men on earth as stars in the sky. At his birth each man receives a star of his own; and when his end draws near, that star falls to earth, the man dies, and his soul floats upward to the clouds. The belief links the hearth-side deathbed to the whole machinery of heaven.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part I ch. 10; not verbatim.

title.en: The Badnjak: Bringing the Christmas Log Home
title.zh: 巴德尼亞克：迎聖誕原木入宅

region.en: Serbia and the South Slavs (symbolic pin at Belgrade)
region.zh: 塞爾維亞與南斯拉夫（象徵性定位於貝爾格勒）

texts.period: Rite recorded 19th c.; pre-Christian in origin (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 2

summary.en: Before sunrise on Christmas Eve the Serbian housefather fetches the badnjak log, clucking like a hen while the children cheep like chicks; the log is greeted, buttered with honey and wine, set on the new fire, and grain is scattered like a sowing for the children to peck — the hearth-genius welcomed home for the new year.
summary.zh: 聖誕前夕日出之前，塞爾維亞家主往林取聖誕原木，口作母雞聲、孩童學雛鳥；原木受迎、抹蜜澆酒，置於新火之上，撒穀如播種讓孩童啄拾——爐靈迎歸，歲歲更新。

sensitivity.note: Living rite; described at ethnographic level.

passages.text: Before sunrise on Christmas Eve the head of a Serbian household goes to the forest for the badnjak, a log of oak, beech, or ash. Doffing his cap he carries it into the room, clucking like a hen while the children stand in a row behind him, cheeping like chickens. With candles burning on either side of the door he walks the log into every corner, the household throwing corn upon him; then he lays the badnjak and a ploughshare by the fireside with honey, butter, and wine, and addresses the log: 'Welcome! Come and eat your supper!'
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 2; not verbatim.

passages.text: When the log burns well the farmer takes a festive bread modelled with animals of dough and a cup of wine to the corn-loft, leaving a portion on its window; then, filling a glove with wheat kernels and a silver coin, he strews the grain over the floor like a sowing, and the children throw themselves upon it picking it up like poultry — whoever finds the coin will have good luck. The hearth-fire, rekindled with the badnjak, renews the year; the log is the special symbol of the genius of the house in his capacity as protector of the hearth.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 2; not verbatim.

title.en: Kupalo Night: Jumping the Fire to Read a Marriage
title.zh: 庫帕洛之夜：躍火以卜姻緣

region.en: Russia and the Slavic lands (symbolic pin at Vilnius)
region.zh: 俄羅斯與斯拉夫諸地（象徵性定位於維爾紐斯）

texts.period: Rite recorded 19th c.; pre-Christian in origin (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 4

summary.en: On St. John's Eve the girls blindfold their prettiest companion — the kupaljo — who deals out garlands: fresh flowers mean a happy marriage, withered ones doom, and her touch means a year unwed; at nightfall couples jump the bonfire hand in hand, and a spark that follows them foretells a wedding.
summary.zh: 聖約翰之夜，少女們蒙住最美者之眼——是為『庫帕洛』——由其分發花環：新鮮者婚美，枯萎者不幸，觸之者一年不嫁；入夜情侶手挽手躍過火堆，火星隨後即兆成婚。

sensitivity.note: Living rite; described at ethnographic level.

passages.text: The Kupalo festival, now coinciding with St. John the Baptist's day, was in origin a domestic celebration of marriage and the admission of new members into the family, its erotic customs joined with funereal commemoration of the ancestors who once presided over such rites. On the morning the girls go to the woods and fields to pick flowers for wreaths.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 4; not verbatim.

passages.text: Choosing the prettiest among them they lead her singing into the forest, blindfold and garland her, and dance about her while she, the kupaljo, picks up garland after garland and deals them out: a fresh wreath promises fortunate wedlock, withered flowers unhappiness. When all garlands are given the girls run away, for any maiden the kupaljo touches is fated to remain unwed for the year.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 4; not verbatim.

passages.text: At twilight a fire is kindled, and the lads and lasses, taking each other's hands, jump over the flame two by two: those who do not loosen hands in jumping will become husband and wife, and the same is predicted by a spark that comes out of the fire after them. Figures of Kupalo and Marena are made and drowned and burned like a Rusalka; in some places Jarilo and Kostroma are buried instead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 4; not verbatim.

title.en: The Rusalye: Dressing the Birch for the Drowned
title.zh: 羅薩利耶：為溺亡者妝點樺樹

region.zh: 大俄羅斯（象徵性定位於弗拉基米爾）

texts.period: Rite recorded 19th c.; pre-Christian in origin (Machal 1918)

source.work: Jan Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 3

summary.en: On Semik the villages go singing into the woods, fell a young birch, dress it in woman's robes and ribbons, and carry it home in procession; a straw doll arrayed in holiday garments is finally thrown into the water or burned — a second funeral to content the Rusalky, the unburied dead of the waters.
summary.zh: 謝米克之日，村人歌行入林，伐幼樺，為之著女衣繫彩帶，列隊迎歸；草偶著節日盛裝，終則投入水中或焚之——此乃二次葬禮，以慰水中介埋之羅薩爾卡亡魂。

sensitivity.note: Living rite; described at ethnographic level.

passages.text: In Russia the Rusalye were celebrated at Whitsuntide. On Whitsun Monday a small shed adorned with garlands, flowers, and fragrant grasses was raised in the centre of an oak grove, a straw doll in holiday garments set inside, and people from all quarters brought food and drink, dancing round the shed in merriment.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 3; not verbatim.

passages.text: On the Thursday before Whitsunday (Semik) the people leave town for the forests singing ancient songs, pick flowers for wreaths, and fell a nice young birch which the lasses dress in woman's robes trimmed with gaudy ribbons. Carrying the tree in procession with festive songs they bring it to a village house, where it stays till Sunday. The doll finally thrown into the water or burned is called a Rusalka, and the ceremony is probably a second funeral meant to secure the favour of the Rusalky — the spirits of those who died violently and were never buried with rites.
passages.note: Paraphrase of Machal, Slavic Mythology, Mythology of All Races III (1918), Part IV ch. 3; not verbatim.
